DISCUSSION ITEM a.
Review of Enacted State Budget Enclosure Abby Benson, Vice President, Administration and Finance The Finance and Facilities Committee reviewed the FY27 state budget approved by the General Assembly on June 9, 2026.
Vice President Abby Benson reported that the General Assembly approved a $4.2 million increase to the operating budget, an amount in line with the Governor’s Recommended Budget (GRB), but well below the University’s request of $37.6 million.
She reminded the Committee of the three categories for the request: Operating Budget Shortfall, Current Service Level, and Strategic Initiatives, of which only the Current Service Level was funded.
She noted that of the $4.2 million increase in the operating budget, $1.3 million of this amount reflects support for corresponding expenses imposed by the state for centralized services.
Strategic Initiatives have not been funded for a number of years, but the University continues to maintain this request to signal the importance of these initiatives.

Change management continues to be a key factor for the implementation.
Over the past several weeks, outreach and engagement efforts have increased to provide opportunities for faculty, staff, and campus stakeholders to learn about the Workday program.
These activities are focused on building awareness, preparing the University community for upcoming changes, and driving adoption to support a successful transition to the new system .
Overall, the project remains on track , however we are mindful and maintain focus on risk management, stakeholder engagement, and organizational readiness.

Overview of the Financial Statements The Universit y’s financial statements are prepared in accordance with GASB principles, focusing on the institution as a whole rather than on individual funds or activities.

The University reports its operations as a business -type activity, utilizing the economic measurement focus and the full accrual basis of accounting.
This approach allows the University to recognize revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, providing a comprehensive view of its financial performance.
As a component unit of the State of Rhode Island, the results of the University’s operations and net position are summarized in the State’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR).
This report is derived from the State’s government -wide financial statements, ensuring transparency and accountability in the University’s financial reporting within the broader context of state finances.
The University’s financial statements consist of three basic components that work together to provide a comprehensive picture of its financial health.
Each statement provides a different perspective: what the University owns and owes, how its financial position changed during the year, and how cash moved into and out of the University. 1.
Statement of Net Position: This statement provides a snapshot of the University’s financial position at the end of the fiscal year.

It reports the University’s assets and deferred outflows of resources, liabilities and deferred inflows of resources, and the resulting net position.
In simple terms, it helps readers understand the resources available to the University and its financial obligations.
Changes in net position over time can provide insight into whether the University’s overall financial position is strengthening or weakening. 2.
Statement of Revenues and Expenses and Changes in Net Position: This statement explains how and why the University’s net position changed during the fiscal year.
It reports revenues earned and expenses incurred during the year, regardless of when the related cash is received or paid.
For example, tuition revenue may be recognized when educational services are provided, even if payment is received later.
Similarly, expenses may be recognized before cash is paid, such as when employees earn leave benefits that will be paid in the future.
The resulting change in net position shows whether the University’s financial activities increased or decreased its net position during the year.

Below is a summary of net tuition and fees received by the University (dollars in millions): Tuition increased by $18.49 million due to an increase in tuition rates of 3.5% for both in-state and out-of-state students coupled with a slight increase in total enrollment of 1.26%.
Housing revenue increased by $3.68 million or 7.29% based on an approximate 1% increase in housing rates and approximate 7% increase in students living on campus.

Dining revenue grew by $3.38 million, driven by an approximate 5% increase in meal plan rates and a student shift toward the purchase of higher-tier plans.
The scholarship allowance increased by $10.27 million or 5.95% mainly due to an increase in the Presidential scholarship of $9.92 million, ultimately reducing net tuition revenue, respectively.
Operating Expenses The operating expenses for the University totaled $706.96 million in fiscal year 2026, up from $685.03 million in 2025.
This represents an increase of $21.93 million, or 3.20%.
A portion of this increase is attributable to the increase in salaries and benefits costs of $ 5.57 million.
This rise reflects both strategic position investments and necessary salary adjustments to support the University’s operational needs, along with cost-of-living salary adjustments ranging from 3.0% to 4.0%.

Other Nonoperating Revenues and Expenses Net nonoperating revenues contributed $105.95 million to the net position.
Net nonoperating revenues improved by $21.57 million over FY25, primarily the result of a $2.88 million private in-kind gift (the Research Vessel Warfish), a reimbursement of $3.53 million of covid-related hotel room costs and an increase of $2.14 million in net investment income .
Additionally, an increase of $9.77 million in combined capital appropriations (RICAP funding) and state contributed capital (GO Bond funding), helped achieve an increase in net nonoperating revenues.

Capital appropriations and gifts included in other net nonoperating revenue totaling $99.54 million for the year ended June 30, 2026 consist of the following: • State Capital Plan Funds: $53.55 million • State Contributed Capital: $40.74 million • Capital Gifts from the Alumni Foundation: $2.37 million • Private Capital Gifts in Kind: $2.88 million Significant Capital Asset and Long-Term Financing Activity Capital Assets The University generally has funded its capital plans through a combination of funds received from University operations, bonds issued by the Rhode Island Health and Educational Building Corporation (RIHEBC), State appropriations, general obligation bonds, federal appropriations, and private fundraising.
The execution of the University’s capital improvement plan is contingent upon approval from the State and sufficient funding.
The Board of Trustees submits a comprehensive five-year capital improvement plan to the General Assembly and the State annually.
For the period covering fiscal years 2027-2031, the University’s capital improvement plan totals $1.91 billion.
